headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors if ms-swift feeds unstructured shared documents or outputs without verification; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via file-based handoff.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ms-swift reads/writes files and processes text, images, and documents; unstructured also reads/writes files and parses documents. If outputs are handed off through shared files, attacker-controlled document content can influence downstream interpretation. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred from file-based interaction.
conditions: IF the two agents exchange content through a shared filesystem or workspace
IF unstructured treats ms-swift-generated files as trusted instructions or metadata
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Strip instructions from documents before handoff
Add a human review step before any file handoff
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to exchanged files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read files and touch sensitive-looking data classes; ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token and sdk-token, while unstructured processes documents and images. A shared workspace could expose secrets or document contents across the pair. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so the risk is inferred rather than direct.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or mounted workspace
IF ms-swift writes secrets or logs into files that unstructured can read
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared folders
Mount separate read/write volumes per agent
Rotate any exposed tokens immediately
Limit unstructured to a document-only input directory
requires-engineering: enforce filesystem ACLs between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files, read files, spawn subprocesses, and install packages. That overlap creates a realistic chance of clobbering shared artifacts or dependency state if they operate in the same workspace. ms-swift does not modify git state, but the shared mutable filesystem is enough for conflict.
conditions: IF both agents write into the same directory tree
IF package installation occurs in a shared environment
mitigations: Give each agent its own working directory
Pin dependencies in separate virtual environments
Serialize writes to shared outputs
Use read-only mounts for inputs
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: ms-swift can generate training, evaluation, or configuration outputs, and unstructured can parse documents from files. If unstructured consumes ms-swift output as authoritative input without verification, errors can cascade into downstream document products. The profiles do not show a verification gate, so the pathway is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF unstructured ingests ms-swift outputs without validation
IF ms-swift outputs are used as source-of-truth for document processing
mitigations: Add schema validation between agents
Require human review of intermediate outputs
Compare outputs against a known-good sample
Log and diff transformations at each step
requires-engineering: implement confidence/provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token and sdk-token and touches datasets, checkpoints, and logs, while unstructured exposes a privacy-policy endpoint and processes documents. This suggests possible retention or residency mismatch, but the profiles do not document a concrete regulatory conflict. The risk is limited to policy alignment checks rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated documents or secrets are processed through both agents
IF their retention or privacy policies differ for the same data class
mitigations: Review both privacy policies before deployment
Avoid sending regulated data through the pair
Set short retention windows for logs and outputs
Document data-class handling per agent
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing and retention controls
